source_title: Blockbuster (retailer) - Wikipedia (decline, Netflix acquisition offer, and 2010 Chapter 11)
publisher_issuer: Wikipedia (tertiary encyclopedia, citing CNBC/Variety/contemporaneous press); figures corroborated by CNBC and contemporaneous reporting
company_context: Blockbuster was the dominant US video-rental retail and franchise chain. It declined an opportunity to acquire Netflix for roughly $50 million around 2000, leaned heavily on late-fee revenue, and was slow to pivot to mail-order and streaming. Peak revenue reached roughly $6.1 billion in 2004; the company filed for Chapter 11 in September 2010 and was effectively wound down over the following years.
business_type: Brick-and-mortar video-rental retail and franchise, large store footprint, demand exposed to streaming substitution
evidence_summary: Blockbuster grew to peak revenue of roughly $6.1 billion in 2004 but failed to adapt to the shift toward mail-order and streaming video, embodied by its reported refusal to acquire Netflix for about $50 million circa 2000. Late fees reportedly generated about $800 million per year, around 16% of revenue, creating an incentive to protect the legacy model rather than cannibalize it with digital alternatives. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on September 23, 2010 with about $900 million in debt amid competition from Netflix, Redbox, and video-on-demand. Its remaining roughly 1,700 stores were acquired by Dish Network in 2011, and the last roughly 300 company-owned stores closed by 2014. This is a classic demand collapse driven by a strategic refusal to disrupt a profitable legacy revenue stream.
